The Big-head Far East goby (Gymnogobius urotaenia) is a benthic fish inhabiting coastal estuaries and brackish tidal creeks of northeastern Asia. Field surveys conducted in the Amur River basin indicate that females produce demersal, adhesive eggs measuring 1.1 mm in length and 0.6 mm in width, corresponding to a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00021 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00021 grams]. Hatchlings emerge as yolk-sac larvae after a relatively short incubation period; at a stable water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], egg hatching occurs at roughly 10 days [ab = roughly 10 days]. This rapid eclosion is typical of small-bodied gobiids, where the endotrophic larva must quickly exhaust its limited yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The chorion rupture event is synchronised with diel tidal cycles, likely an adaptation to disperse prolarvae into productive nursery zones where copepod nauplii are abundant.

Sexual maturation in Gymnogobius urotaenia is attained at a relatively modest size compared to many congeners. Based on dissection of over two hundred specimens from the Peter the Great Bay region, the total length at puberty was determined to be 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters]. This milestone corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis in females and active spermatogenesis in males, typically occurring during the second calendar year of life. Individuals below this threshold are classified as immature sub-adults, possessing undifferentiated gonads and showing no evidence of prior spawning activity. The 8 centimeter pubertal length is consistent with an early-maturing life history strategy, likely advantageous in dynamic estuarine environments where adult mortality risks from piscivorous birds and larger predatory fish are elevated. Post-pubertal fish invest heavily in somatic growth before their first reproductive event.

The species exhibits a maximum recorded ultimate total length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters], a value documented from a single large male collected in the Razdolnaya River estuary. This asymptotic size is notably smaller than that of its sympatric congener Gymnogobius castaneus, which can exceed 25 centimeters, suggesting a life history trade-off favouring early reproduction over continued somatic expansion. Growth trajectories derived from otolith increment analysis show that most adults plateau near 15 to 16 centimeters, with the 17.5 centimeter maximum representing an exceptional outlier rather than a typical endpoint. Larger individuals are disproportionately represented among nest-guarding males, who must defend cavities under cobbles against conspecific intruders during the spawning season.

Longevity records for the Big-head Far East goby, derived from mark-recapture studies in stable cold-water habitats, indicate a remarkable lifespan when held at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]: the oldest documented individual survived for 6 years [am = 6 years]. This extended lifespan is uncommon among small gobiids, many of which are annual or biennial species, and likely reflects the low metabolic demands of the cool, oligotrophic waters characteristic of the northern Sea of Japan coastline. Senescence in this population manifests as a gradual decline in condition factor and a marked reduction in gonadosomatic index among fish older than five years. Field observations confirm that reproductive output diminishes after the fourth year, though sporadic spawning events may occur in the terminal year before natural mortality intervenes.

Comparing the early life history to the adult phase reveals a striking contrast in pace. The brief yolk-dependent larval stage, lasting approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] at a water temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], produces a prolarva weighing just 0.00021 grams [Wwb = 0.00021 grams], yet this tiny individual must locate suitable prey within a few days of yolk-sac resorption or face starvation. The transition from a 0.00021 gram hatchling to a sexually mature fish of 8 centimeters [Lp = 8 centimeters] requires a several-thousand-fold increase in wet mass, achieved through a protracted juvenile growth period. The ultimate size ceiling of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters] and the 6-year maximum lifespan (6 years) [am = 6 years] together define a life history envelope that prioritises persistent adult survival and iteroparous reproduction over a single, high-investment spawning event at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C].
